items.t: Federal Reserve announces College Fed Challenge winners
body: The University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) won the 23rd annual national College Fed Challenge on Friday, a team competition that encourages undergraduate students to learn about the U.S. economy, monetary policymaking, and the role of the Federal Reserve System. Teams analyze economic and financial conditions and formulate a monetary policy recommendation, modeling the Federal Open Market Committee. The team, from Los Angeles, California, represented the San Francisco District and included Aarushi Maheshwari, Annika Chan, Atul Prasanth, Caitlyn Cox, Finn Karish, Eli Brooks (alternate), Kennedy Yang (alternate), Manasi Vartak (alternate), Ronojoy Borpujari (alternate), and Sahil Sudani (alternate). The team's advisers were Chris Surro and Ali Haider Ismail.

"I am very happy to congratulate the students who competed in this year's College Fed Challenge, especially the winners and finalists," said Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh. "They took on the same big questions we policymakers face. I'm impressed by their talent, their rigor, and their eagerness to think hard about monetary policy and the economy."

This year's College Fed Challenge included 141 schools from 34 states across the nation, the most in the competition's history. Teams submitted video presentations or participated in local competitions last month. Twenty-one semi-finalist teams then participated in question-and-answer sessions held earlier this month, and seven finalists were invited to the Federal Reserve Board for the national finals. The other national finalists were the University of Chicago in second place and the University of Maryland, College Park in third place. Teams with honorable mentions include Cleveland State University, Harvard College, Pennsylvania State University, and St. Lawrence University.
Teams were evaluated on their economic analysis, responses to the judges' questions, teamwork, and presentations.

items.x: Speech At the XXIX Annual Conference of the Central Bank of Chile, Santiago, Chile
body: Thank you, Governor Costa, for that kind introduction and for the invitation to deliver this keynote address and to participate in the 29th Annual Conference of the Central Bank of Chile today.1 It is a distinct privilege to be back in Santiago. I first came to Chile between my second and third years as a Ph.D. student at Berkeley after completing a summer as an intern at the World Bank. I was on a quest to determine whether economic growth in Latin America or in another region of the world would be the subject of my dissertation. It piqued my interest in inflation targeting, a sound fiscal framework, and now, of course, how to think about the economic forces reshaping the global economy. I am grateful for the chance to continue to learn from your experience and to share some of my own thinking.

I want to begin by acknowledging a fact that may seem obvious but is easy to overlook in the day-to-day work of setting monetary policy: The U.S. economy does not sit in isolation. As a member of the Federal Reserve Board of Governors, my mandate is domestic—to promote maximum employment and price stability in the United States. But achieving that mandate requires that I pay careful attention to global developments, including economic and financial developments in Chile and across Latin America. The forces reconfiguring your economies are, in many cases, identical to the forces reconfiguring ours, even if they arrive on our respective shores somewhat differently.

Geopolitics and Trade Let me start with geopolitical events. Over the past several years, the global economy has absorbed a remarkable sequence of shocks. Russia's war in Ukraine disrupted energy and commodity markets worldwide. The conflict in the Middle East pushed up energy prices again this year, and experts have warned that damaged infrastructure and depleted inventories could keep oil prices elevated for an extended period. These are not simply North American concerns. Oil is a globally traded commodity, and a conflict that drives up the price of oil in Houston drives it up in Santiago, as well. The precise transmission differs across countries, depending on whether they are net energy importers or exporters, but few economies have been insulated.

A related story applies to trade. Over the past two years, the U.S. has raised tariffs on a wide range of imports, and considerable uncertainty remains about where tariff levels will ultimately settle. In the U.S., the effects of tariffs on inflation appear to have moderated, even as uncertainty about future trade policy persists. China, too, has increased trade restrictions, limiting exports of critical minerals for which it supplies a large fraction of the world's production. These minerals are a crucial input, and uncertainty is rising around the world about access to them. I raise this not to make a judgment about trade policy—that is not my role—but because such shifts inevitably reverberate across the global economy. When trade relationships between major economies are altered, other countries must decide how to respond: whether to deepen commercial ties elsewhere, reconfigure supply chains, or wait for greater clarity before committing to new investment. These are decisions playing out in boardrooms and finance ministries around the world right now, including, I suspect, in some of the economies represented in this room.

The Global AI Buildout The third global force I want to highlight—and the one I will spend the most time on—is the extraordinary buildout of artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure now underway around the world.

body: Worldwide employment by U.S. multinational enterprises increased 0.9 percent to 44.2 million workers in 2024 (preliminary) from 43.8 million workers in 2023 (revised), according to statistics released today by the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis on the operations and finances of U.S. parent companies and their majority-owned foreign affiliates.

Employment in the United States by U.S. parents increased 0.1 percent to 29.9 million workers in 2024. U.S. parents accounted for 67.6 percent of worldwide employment by U.S. multinational enterprises (MNEs), down from 68.1 percent in 2023. Employment abroad by foreign affiliates of U.S. MNEs increased 2.7 percent to 14.3 million workers and accounted for 32.4 percent of employment by U.S. MNEs worldwide.

U.S. parents accounted for 21.7 percent of total private industry employment in the United States in 2024, down from 21.9 percent in 2023. Employment by U.S. parents was largest in manufacturing, in “other industries,” led by transportation and warehousing, and in retail trade. Employment abroad by foreign affiliates was largest in India, Mexico, and the United Kingdom.

Worldwide current-dollar value added of U.S. MNEs increased 8.0 percent to $7.4 trillion in 2024. Value added by U.S. parents, a measure of U.S. parents’ direct contribution to U.S. gross domestic product, increased 8.5 percent to $5.7 trillion. U.S parents accounted for 21.8 percent of total U.S. private-industry value added, up from 21.2 percent in 2023. Foreign affiliate value added increased 6.5 percent to $1.8 trillion. Value added by foreign affiliates was largest in the United Kingdom, Ireland, and Canada.

Worldwide expenditures for property, plant, and equipment of U.S. MNEs increased 7.1 percent to $1.2 trillion. Expenditures by U.S. parents accounted for $968.7 billion, representing 36.5 percent of all U.S. private-business capital expenditures. Expenditures by foreign affiliates accounted for $216.2 billion.

Worldwide research and development (R&D) expenditures of U.S. MNEs increased 10.1 percent to $622.7 billion. U.S. parents accounted for expenditures of $536.5 billion, representing 69.6 percent of business R&D performed in the United States. Foreign affiliates accounted for expenditures of $86.2 billion.

Additional statistics on the activities of U.S. parent companies and their foreign affiliates, including sales, balance sheet and income statement items, compensation of employees, trade in goods, and more are available on BEA’s website. More industry detail for U.S. parents and more industry and country detail for foreign affiliates are also available on the website.
Statistics for 2023 were revised to incorporate newly available and revised source data. Preliminary statistics for 2023 were released in August 2025.

items.x: Speech At the 2026 College Fed Challenge Finals, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Washington, D.C.
body: Thank you, Robin, and welcome, students and teachers, to the Federal Reserve Board.1

We are gathered for the finals of the annual College Fed Challenge, a tradition begun 23 years ago under Chairman Alan Greenspan. The challenge is to prepare and present a monetary policy recommendation that will best promote the Federal Reserve's dual mandate of stable prices and maximum sustainable employment. Students on the seven teams that will compete today represent the University of California, Los Angeles; the University of Chicago; Cleveland State University; Harvard College; the University of Maryland, College Park; Pennsylvania State University; and St. Lawrence University.

Let me start by congratulating all of the students here today, and your faculty advisers, for advancing to the finals by winning preliminary rounds of the competition. A record 141 schools participated this year, from 34 states. It is incredibly gratifying to think of the number of young people motivated to learn about the Federal Reserve's role in promoting a healthy economy.

A few weeks from now, my colleagues on the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) and I will be sitting at this same table, facing the same challenge you face today. Like you, we will be examining publicly available data on economic and financial conditions and will apply our understanding of how monetary policy influences those conditions to render our best judgment of the policy stance that best furthers the Fed's goals.

Crucial to that decision will be clearly explaining the Committee's actions and intentions to the public—the same task that you will face later this morning, when you present your recommendations to our judges. As I hope you have learned, clear communication is essential because monetary policy works to a considerable extent by influencing the public's view of current and future economic and financial conditions.

Monetary policy has evolved since this competition began in 2003. At that time, the FOMC relied on a single tool to influence financial conditions and the broader economy—it set a target for the federal funds rate. In the years since, the Committee expanded its toolkit with unconventional policy tools.

In an important way, the competition you will engage in today is very much like what the FOMC does at its meetings. On December 8, my 18 FOMC colleagues and I will each present our view of the economic outlook, and on December 9, our view of the proper stance of monetary policy. Before we express those views to the public, we communicate with each other, presenting evidence, testing hypotheses, and making arguments that will ultimately help us arrive at a consensus that is summarized in our postmeeting statement. Every monetary policy speech I give has its origins in this room, in the argument I make here, and the extent to which that argument holds up to what I hear from my colleagues. When I engage in the essential task of explaining monetary policy to the public, I am really doing the same thing that I do here at FOMC meetings. And very much what you will do today. Present the evidence. Make an argument. Persuade.

I hope your preparations for this event have added to your understanding of the economy and the Federal Reserve's role and perhaps will even spur some of you to pursue further study of economics and finance. Among the talented individuals who are participating in today's challenge, I hope there are some who may one day contribute to our understanding of the economy and the work of the Fed. But I hope that all of you have benefited from this experience by adding to your knowledge and developing research, analytical, and communication skills that will help you in whatever careers you choose.

items.t: Christine Lagarde: Acting in time
body: It is a pleasure to be back at this congress. This is the eighth time I have spoken here as President of the ECB, and it will sadly be the last.
In preparing for today, I reread those speeches. The topics have varied, from growth and inflation to capital markets and the Single Market.
But one concern runs through all of them: how to make Europe stronger, so that its prosperity is driven by its own strengths and less exposed to decisions taken elsewhere.

For many years, the challenges we discussed here were old ones. We had fallen short of our ambitions for the Single Market. Our growth relied too heavily on external demand for an economy of our size, and our competitiveness was slowly eroding.

Those challenges have not gone away. But in recent years, new ones have been layered on top. Dependencies that we once saw as a normal part of an open economy, from critical raw materials to technology, can now be used against us. That has made economic sovereignty a challenge in its own right.
The old challenges and the new ones have something in common.
Five centuries ago, Machiavelli compared the problems of states to a fever that, at the start, is “easy to cure but difficult to detect” and, in time, becomes “easy to detect but difficult to cure”.
Both kinds of challenge are of this sort. By the time everyone can see the need to act, the best time to act has usually passed.

Acting early, before the case is obvious, is one of the hardest things a policymaker has to do. It means paying a price up front for a distant pay-off. And if nothing goes wrong, those who acted can easily appear to have paid that price for nothing.
Today I would like to reflect on how Europe can still act early, drawing on how we have approached this at the ECB and on what I have learned along the way.

It is often said that Europe only moves in a crisis. Jean Monnet wrote that Europe would be forged in crises, and would be the sum of the solutions adopted for them. The idea was that Europe has a kind of in-built inertia that only a crisis can overcome.
My experience of the past seven years is that this is only partly true. Europe responds decisively to some crises and hesitantly to others.
When events convince us that the world has changed, we act. During my term, I have watched Europe break one taboo after another.

Before the pandemic, few believed that the EU would ever borrow on a large scale in its own name. But once we accepted that no country could recover on its own, we created a recovery fund financed by common debt to the tune of €800 billion.

Europe was also said to be unable to take its own security seriously. Yet when Germany concluded that it would have to take on more of its own defence, it made the biggest change to its defence spending in generations. At the European level, we also agreed on Security Action for Europe (SAFE), which offers up to €150 billion in loans for joint defence procurement. And after decades of neutrality, Finland and Sweden joined NATO.

Nor did many expect Europe to act as a geopolitical power. Yet it is now Ukraine’s largest supporter. And when it became clear that Europe would have to bear more of the cost, the countries ready to act found a new way to borrow together on Ukraine’s behalf, even though not every country was ready to take part. Hence the coalition of the willing.

What made these steps possible? In each case, the cost of inaction was there for all to see, and it was plainly greater than the cost of acting. Once we were convinced of that, our institutions did not hold us back.

Our difficulties arise when a crisis moves slowly. The cost of inaction is then just as real, but it is far less visible. It builds up a little each year, and no single moment forces a decision. Meanwhile, the cost of acting is certain and has to be paid straight away.
Both the old challenges and the new ones are of this kind.
Take capital markets. We have all agreed for more than a decade that Europe needs a capital markets union. But building it means taking on vested interests now, for gains that arrive years later.

items.t: Jefferson, Monetary Policy amid Frequent and Complex Shocks
items.x: Speech At the International Monetary Fund and Central Bank of Brazil Conference “A Quarter Century of Inflation Targeting in Latin America: Progress, Challenges, and the Road Ahead,” Brasília, Brazil
body: Thank you, Nigel, for that kind introduction, and thank you to the Central Bank of Brazil and International Monetary Fund for hosting this important conference.1 It is an honor to be here with my fellow panelists. Today, I will briefly discuss issues that are critical for central bankers around the world—that is, how to assess and confront economic shocks. I discussed these issues in more depth in a speech earlier this year at Stanford University.2

Shocks, by their nature, are difficult to predict and vary in length, but we are nonetheless very familiar with them. Just in the past few years, we have experienced a pandemic, a rapid rise in energy prices associated with geopolitical tensions, changes to trade policy, and a technological breakthrough. One way to classify shocks is to determine whether their initial effect is on the demand side or the supply side of the economy. Demand shocks affect spending by households, businesses, or the government without changing productive capacity. Supply shocks change productive capacity—what economists call "potential output"—by affecting the available supply of labor and capital or the productivity of those inputs. The nature and duration of these shocks influence the approach to monetary policymaking.

As a monetary policymaker in the United States, I must consider whether and how shocks impact both sides of our dual mandate—maximum employment and stable prices. When a shock moves the output gap and inflation in the same direction, our objectives are aligned, and policy actions taken to address one also support the other.3 When a shock pushes them in opposite directions, there is a tradeoff. The recent rise in oil prices tied to the conflict in the Middle East is an example of the latter. An energy price shock can push up inflation while weighing on real incomes and demand. The appropriate response depends on the relative costs of missing each objective and the balance of risks. When the recent energy price shock occurred, inflation in the U.S. was already above our 2 percent target. If inflation expectations risk becoming unanchored, a stronger reaction to inflation is warranted. If price pressures are contained, it may be prudent to prioritize downside risks to employment.

Shocks that affect both aggregate supply and aggregated demand but with differential timing are especially challenging for monetary policymakers. The rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) represents such a shock. Business adoption of AI has risen considerably over the past two years.4 On the demand side, optimism about the technology has been boosting business investment in data centers, advanced computing equipment, and related products. On the supply side, AI is likely to automate some tasks and augment others, which could raise productivity and, in turn, the growth rate of potential output. Currently, the AI buildout is exerting upward pressure on demand and inflation. In the future, advancements in productivity could exert downward pressure on inflation while continuing to support growth. Labor market effects are relevant as well. AI could cause some job displacement, a meaningful challenge for affected households. Like many technological breakthroughs of the past, however, AI could lead to the creation of new jobs and new firms that we have not yet imagined.

Shocks do not arrive in a vacuum. Energy, trade, and AI shocks are all unfolding at once. My colleagues at the Fed and my peers around the world must weigh them simultaneously. Our task is to remain attentive to our respective mandates and to keep the stance of our policies appropriately calibrated to achieve those stated goals. For the U.S. economy, my goal is to restore price stability while maintaining a solid labor market. That outcome will help the economy grow according to its full potential.
Thank you, and I look forward to our discussion.
1. The views expressed here are my own and are not necessarily those of my colleagues on the Federal Open Market Committee or the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System. Return to text

items.t: Barr, Investing in America’s Underserved Communities
items.x: Speech At Making Missing Markets: Catalyzing Capital and Igniting Innovation, Federal Reserve Bank of New York, New York, New York
body: Thank you to the New York Fed and the organizers of this conference for the opportunity to speak to you today.1 For two reasons I can think of, New York is an excellent place to discuss ways to increase investments in communities where incomplete or missing markets have resulted in less investment than needed. First, it makes sense to initiate a conversation about incentivizing private investment in the center of American finance. Second, New York has been successful over the past few decades in attracting investment in lower-income neighborhoods, reversing forces that once made parts of this city synonymous with urban decline. I first saw that for myself 30 years ago, touring the South Bronx with Treasury Secretary Bob Rubin, where public–private partnerships were building housing, creating businesses and jobs, and making streets safer, block by block. That progress has continued, and the strategies and partnerships we will be discussing today have been a major engine for that success.

The backdrop for community investment, of course, is the economy—how fast it is growing, how well it is creating jobs, and how well incomes are keeping up with the cost of living. So I will start with the economic outlook. Overall, the economy is strong, with low unemployment, solid consumer spending, and robust business investment. But inflation is too high, making it hard for American families to make ends meet. Many families are struggling. And that's why it is so important for the Fed to bring inflation back down to our target of 2 percent in a timely way. If the economy evolves as I currently forecast, I expect it will be appropriate to raise rates further to achieve that goal on behalf of the American people. Of course, I'll continue to monitor the incoming data, the evolving forecast, and the balance of risks in making that assessment.

Strong and sustainable communities are key to American prosperity. When a community is strong and resilient, people see a future there and invest in that future—they buy homes, shop locally, and start new businesses. When hard times hit resilient communities, people can weather the storm and bounce back in part because they believe that they and their communities will bounce back—that jobs and opportunities will return. That's why we at the Fed are committed to building stronger communities. And while economic activity and employment are continuing to grow for the country as a whole, not all families and communities are thriving. Far from it. Wealthier households are doing well, but middle- and lower-income households are struggling, and the economy is leaving some communities behind. Recent estimates are that 44 percent of Americans live in low-income communities, where a fifth or more of people live below the poverty line.2 These communities often lack sufficient investment in housing, business, and infrastructure.

The Fed's recent Survey of Consumer Finances confirms that the majority of households has very little wealth.3 And lower-wealth households are nearly four times as likely to say that they cannot rely on friends and family for financial help or provide that help themselves.4 Think about how that inability to help, or get help, can reverberate across a community. When jobs and opportunities lag in a community, it eats away at the ties that connect families and neighbors. The dignity of work is so key to how many people try to navigate these difficult times, yet in many communities, despite a strong economy, some people are finding it hard to find a good-paying job.

body: Today, the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis released new statistics measuring the outdoor recreation economy for the nation, all 50 states, and the District of Columbia. The new data show that the value added of the outdoor recreation economy accounted for 2.3 percent ($704.2 billion) of current-dollar gross domestic product (GDP) for the nation in 2025 (national table 2). Across states and the District of Columbia, value added for outdoor recreation as a share of state GDP ranged from 6.1 percent in Hawaii to 1.0 percent in the District of Columbia (state table 1).

Inflation-adjusted (“real”) GDP for the outdoor recreation economy increased 1.9 percent in 2025, compared with an increase of 2.3 percent for the overall U.S. economy, reflecting a deceleration from the 2.5 percent increase in 2024 (national table 1). In 2025, real gross output for the outdoor recreation economy increased 2.1 percent, compensation increased 4.6 percent, and employment increased 1.7 percent (national table 9).

Outdoor recreation employment increased in 43 states and the District of Columbia in 2025. The change in outdoor recreation employment ranged from 5.0 percent in Rhode Island, Kansas, and the District of Columbia to −1.1 percent in New Jersey and Alabama (BEA interactive tables).

Outdoor recreation by activity Outdoor recreation activities fall into three general categories: (1) conventional activities such as bicycling, boating, hiking, and hunting; (2) other activities such as gardening and outdoor concerts; and (3) supporting activities such as construction, travel and tourism, local trips, and government expenditures. In 2025, conventional outdoor recreation accounted for 29.2 percent of U.S. outdoor recreation value added, compared with 29.1 percent in 2024. “Other outdoor recreation” accounted for 19.3 percent of value added in 2025, compared with 19.1 percent in 2024. Supporting outdoor recreation accounted for 51.5 percent of value added in 2025, compared with 51.7 percent in 2024.
Additional highlights for value added by activity for 2025 include (state table 2):

Outdoor recreation by industry The outdoor recreation by industry data show the contributions of industries to the outdoor recreation economy, including their impact on value added, gross output, employment, and compensation.

For the nation, the arts, entertainment, recreation, accommodation, and food services industry group was the largest contributor to U.S. outdoor recreation in 2025, accounting for $179.5 billion, or 25.5 percent of current-dollar value added. At the state level, arts, entertainment, recreation, accommodation, and food services was the largest contributor to outdoor recreation value added in 25 states and the District of Columbia. The states with the largest contributions were California ($23.5 billion), Florida ($23.4 billion), and New York ($11.6 billion) (state table 3).

Retail trade was the second-largest industry group for the nation, at $166.5 billion, or 23.6 percent of value added, and was the largest industry group in 22 states. The states with the largest contributions were California ($19.5 billion), Texas ($14.6 billion), and Florida ($13.3 billion).

Transportation and warehousing was the third-largest industry group for the nation, at $86.4 billion, or 12.3 percent of value added, and was the largest industry group in Alaska. The states with the largest contributions were Florida ($12.8 billion), California ($10.8 billion), and Texas ($7.1 billion).

Annual update of outdoor recreation economic statistics Estimates for 2021 to 2024 were updated to incorporate newly available and revised source data. At the national level, gross output, value added, employment, and compensation reflect the results of the 2026 annual update of the National Economic Accounts, which include the National Income and Product Accounts and the Industry Economic Accounts. The state statistics now reflect these updated national data as well as the 2026 annual update of the Regional Economic Accounts and newly available and revised regional source data.
Previously published estimates are available in BEA’s Data Archive.

items.t: Boris Vujčić: Financial Stability Review - November 2026
Risks from AI valuations, fiscal imbalances and geoeconomic tensions weigh on financial stability outlook
body: The outlook for euro area financial stability is being shaped by risks stemming from artificial intelligence (AI) valuations, fiscal imbalances and geoeconomic tensions, according to the November 2026 Financial Stability Review, which is published today by the European Central Bank (ECB).

“Risks to euro area financial stability remain elevated, given persistent geoeconomic uncertainty and growing exposure to AI,” said ECB Vice-President Boris Vujčić. “Banks are well placed to withstand shocks, while vulnerabilities are more pronounced in certain non-banks where risks are growing and macroprudential safeguards are less developed.”

The euro area economy has continued to demonstrate resilience despite an energy shock, trade frictions and extreme weather events. Prolonged energy supply disruptions and persistent trade policy uncertainty could, however, test this resilience.

Enthusiasm about the transformational potential of AI has driven strong gains in global equity markets, despite some recent volatility. Current valuations rely on ambitious earnings expectations which could yet be challenged by financing concerns or by competition from cheaper AI models. Investment in AI infrastructure is increasingly funded through debt, such that a potential change in sentiment could spread losses from equity markets to bond markets.

In the euro area, elevated debt levels, growing sovereign borrowing needs and shifts towards more news-sensitive and leveraged investors in euro area sovereign bonds are increasing the risk of abrupt repricing episodes, although markets have continued to function in an orderly manner. Geoeconomic uncertainty, higher energy prices and weak economic growth could further strain public finances, allowing governments less room to respond to shocks.

Banks’ and non-banks’ exposures to AI financing and sovereign bonds leave them exposed to repricing risks. While bank asset quality remains sound, higher energy prices and weaker economic conditions could make it harder for households and firms to repay their debts. Closer links between banks and non-banks could spread and amplify shocks across the financial system.

The euro area banking sector is well positioned to absorb potential shocks, underpinned by strong profits, solid capital buffers and ample liquidity. Preserving bank resilience remains a key macroprudential priority, alongside addressing vulnerabilities related to liquidity and high levels of borrowing among some non-banks. Accelerating progress on the EU’s savings and investments union will also be essential to support economic growth and competitiveness while preserving financial stability.

items.t: Waller, Considerations at the Intersection of Payments and Tokenized Markets
items.x: Speech At “Navigating the Future of Banking and Payments,” The Clearing House Annual Conference 2026, New York, New York
body: Thank you for inviting me to return and speak today.1 I am delighted to be here during a transformational time in payments. Two years ago, I spoke at The Clearing House's annual conference, where I discussed the roles that the private sector and the Federal Reserve play in payments.2 I argued that the public and private sectors have distinct but complementary roles. In particular, I emphasized that the private sector, through competition, is best positioned to develop solutions that benefit businesses and consumers and to fulfill a clear market need.

The Federal Reserve can support these solutions by providing core payment and settlement infrastructure upon which the private sector can innovate, assessing potential risks to financial stability, and regularly engaging with the industry to better understand market challenges. Related to this last role, it's important to note that my remarks today are informed by rich, ongoing discussions I conduct with industry participants across a variety of forums, including a recent payments innovation roundtable I hosted at the Federal Reserve with participants from across traditional and decentralized finance, or DeFi.3

Turning to the timely themes of the conference, many of the sessions focused on the evolving payments landscape, including the state of competition, technological advancements, and readiness for the future. With this backdrop in mind, today I will discuss some considerations for tokenization in the payment system with an eye toward the future and, in particular, the intersection of this technological advancement with existing systems and markets. To be clear, in this context, my focus is on the concept that a financial instrument can be represented digitally in "token" form and transacted on a new platform or technology, such as a distributed ledger technology like blockchain.4

Although the terms "blockchain," "tokenization," and "smart contract" are widely used, to ensure we are on the same page, I want to give a simple explanation of each of these concepts. A blockchain is simply a database that can have a variety of management properties, such as who can hold a copy of the database, who can read the database, who can change the database, and how the database can be updated. The word block means data are added to the existing database in "blocks"—much like adding a new sheet of data to an existing Excel file.5

Tokenization refers to the process of altering the properties of one form of an asset so that it can be transferred and used on a different platform than its current one. For example, if you go to a casino, you cannot use physical currency at the tables or machines. But you can take your cash and buy poker chips to use on the tables. In this world, poker chips are a tokenized version of physical cash that can be used instead of cash.

Finally, a smart contract is simply a piece of code that is embedded in the database and can be triggered to execute an action at a given point of time or under a particular set of conditions. The key aspect of a smart contract is that all conditions of the code must be met simultaneously for the action to occur and be recorded on the blockchain. Smart contracts allow financial trades to be programmable, which is appealing for automating trades.

In any financial trades on a blockchain, there is an object being bought (say, a tokenized share of stock) and there is a tokenized payment instrument being used to settle the trade. For example, stablecoins are starting to be used behind the scenes to settle obligations among participants in card networks. And The Clearing House is one of several groups building a network for clearing and settling tokenized deposits, which are digital transformations of the digits in your checking account that can then be used as a payment instrument to execute a blockchain trade.

items.t: Warsh, Opening Remarks
items.x: Speech At the Productivity and Jobs Task Force Conference, hosted by the Federal Reserve Board and the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, San Francisco, California
body: I'm grateful to Mary and her colleagues for helping to arrange this gathering. This is my very first visit to a Reserve Bank as Chairman. I wouldn't call it a snap inspection, but I'm certainly impressed. Everything I see reflects high expectations and the inquiring, forward-looking spirit that we need in the Federal Reserve System.

It's good to have Fed colleagues with us from around the country. Central banking is a team sport, and I'm pleased you're here. This conference is an expression of the mission we all serve: One Fed. Fit for Purpose. Focused on the Future.

I also want to thank Marc, Chad, and Asha for leading our Productivity and Jobs Task Force. You're giving the scarcest of resources—your time and your commitment. It's a service to the Fed and to our nation, and I'm grateful.

This task force is one of five I have convened as Chairman. These groups are a way of broadening our thinking . . . of inviting robust discussions that take us further and deeper than fleeting data points or daily market moves. Our task forces are an intellectual investment to better equip us for the next policy conjuncture and beyond.

The common attributes of Asha, Marc, and Chad, the reason I asked them to lead, is not just their exceptional insight and experience. It's their battlefield bravery in the world of ideas . . . their intellect and their willingness to think hard about what might happen next. They, in turn, asked me to open the task force discussion to a wide cross section of stakeholders—and that's the purpose of this conference.

As for me, I always feel energized to be in this part of California. I arrived here way back in 1988 as a Stanford undergrad. I remember sitting in Green Library over Thanksgiving break during my freshman year, reading and wrestling with great works from a canon that I had scarcely known existed, beginning my initiation into the world of ideas. It was a special time to be in the Bay Area—neither boom nor bust, a quieter period between tech surges. And, today, just as I was then, I'm keen to listen to and learn from the great people and first-rate minds around me.

The current era may be the most transformational period in my adult lifetime, marked by the arrival of the general-purpose technology called "super intelligence." SI is an entirely new force in economic life and society. It demands our special attention.

Even a few years ago, the idea that we could have, in our pockets, instant access to genius-level intelligence on almost any subject would have seemed far fetched. Today, with the advances of SI, it's happening. The marginal cost of satisfying limitless curiosity—on questions large and small—is falling fast, perhaps even trending toward zero.

In the tradition of endogenous growth theory in economics, ideas are the ultimate resource. If living standards are to advance, conditions must be favorable to the generation of new ideas. It should be no surprise, then, that the United States is leading. Societies that bring forth the best ideas tend to prosper most. The implications for economic policy can hardly be overstated.

While an idea can be costly to discover, it's free to use. And because an idea is nonrival—that is, one person's use doesn't diminish anyone else's—its value grows with the number of people who use it. The Nobel laureate Paul Romer, among others, has shown that a doubling of ideas and other key inputs can more than double output, allowing increasing returns to scale.1

Even so, in the U.S. over the past several decades, breakthrough ideas have been harder to find. By some estimates, research efforts have increased more than 20 times since the 1930s. Yet, as Nick Bloom, Chad Jones, and their coauthors have pointed out, "Research productivity has fallen by an even larger amount."2 The result: Productivity growth has fluctuated, and in recent quarters, it's been reasonably strong. But it hasn't yet broken out definitively and structurally to the upside.

items.t: Frank Elderson: Smart supervision for small banks
body: Germany’s small and regional banks are trusted partners to the Mittelstand and households across the country, often drawing on deep-rooted relationships in their communities. They play an important role in financing the real economy and support jobs and investment in the regions they serve.

This reflects a broader European reality. Across Europe, a diverse banking sector – combining a range of business models, sizes and areas of expertise – helps ensure that households and businesses can access the financing they need.

As Europe searches for ways to strengthen its long-term growth and competitiveness, these banks will continue to play an important role. But they are very different from large, internationally active banking groups: their business models are often simpler, their activities more focused and their risk profiles less complex. A regulatory and supervisory framework that recognises those differences can support both resilience and competitiveness.

This is already partly the case. The EU prudential framework recognises the diversity of EU banks through the concept of proportionality: the idea that regulatory requirements and supervisory practices should reflect a bank’s size, complexity and risk profile, while maintaining high standards that protect depositors and the stability of our financial system.

This framework already covers a large share of Europe’s smaller banks. Today, around 75% of the banks supervised by national authorities in the euro area – more than 1,400 institutions – qualify as small and non-complex, and thus benefit from proportionate treatment. In Germany, that share is even higher: 81%. Among other things, these banks need only report up to 30% of the data reported by their larger counterparts. Supervisors also tailor the frequency and intensity of their oversight to the complexity and risk profile of each bank.

At the same time, experience gained from applying the framework over recent years has shown that some smaller banks still face regulatory requirements and supervisory practices that were originally designed with much larger and more complex institutions in mind. A more tailored approach would allow supervisors to focus on the risks that matter most while reducing unnecessary complexity for banks.

Over recent months, the ECB and national supervisors have examined where oversight can be simplified without compromising resilience. The result is a set of practical proposals aimed at making oversight for smaller banks more risk-focused, efficient and effective. Rather than creating a new framework, the proposals build on the one already in place for small and non-complex banks. The goal is simple: to preserve the same high standards of safety and soundness while reducing unnecessary complexity.

One important step would be to broaden the range of institutions eligible for the existing framework. To qualify today, a bank must have a balance sheet of less than €5 billion. But experience has shown that size alone does not necessarily make a bank more complex. In Germany, for example, a wave of consolidation among smaller and regional banks has created larger institutions without necessarily making their business models riskier or more complex. In fact, greater scale can help these banks benefit from lower cost-to-income ratios, become more efficient and invest in key areas like digitalisation and cybersecurity.

Amending the regulation to allow national authorities to raise the threshold to €10 billion, where warranted by the bank’s risk profile and the structure of its domestic banking sector, would therefore enable more banks to benefit from proportionate treatment.

Another key change would be to redefine what “non-complex” actually means. Today, some banks are excluded from the framework for largely technical reasons related to resolution planning, rather than reasons of genuine complexity.
Together, these regulatory changes would bring an additional 150 or so banks under the small and non-complex umbrella, making them eligible for more proportionate treatment.

items.t: Barr, Some Potential Financial Stability Implications of Artificial Intelligence
items.x: Speech At the Seventh Annual Association for Computing Machinery International Conference on Artificial Intelligence in Finance, Milan, Italy
body: Thank you for the opportunity to speak to you today.1 This is the fourth speech I have given in the past year devoted exclusively to artificial intelligence (AI), and most of the others have also addressed it in some way. The effects of AI on people and economies around the globe are among the most important issues we are facing today.

Let me stipulate at the outset that I am an optimist about the long-term promise of AI to empower individuals, businesses, and institutions across society. I remain hopeful that if we manage today's challenges and tomorrow's potential disruptions forcefully and effectively, that AI will lift up people, make them more productive, and broadly raise living standards—that most people will learn more and earn more. One of the reasons I'm optimistic about this technology is that I'm also optimistic about the capacity of society to understand and respond to the changes that AI will bring—to engage in a constructive dialogue about ensuring that the benefits from AI are not overwhelmed by the disruptions it will inevitably bring and the risks it may pose.

This conference is part of that dialogue, directed at questions that I believe will be crucial in ensuring that AI is a positive force in the financial system that empowers individuals to better manage their finances and access credit and services, lowers costs and enhances the capabilities of financial service providers, and also makes markets function more effectively. But AI can only succeed in strengthening our financial system in this way if it also supports financial stability, something that is indispensable to a healthy economy.

As has been the case for some time, there are important insights about AI and financial stability in the Federal Reserve's latest Financial Stability Report (FSR) issued on Friday. This edition of the twice-yearly report focuses on the AI investment boom and research by the Fed's staff to assess the degree of leverage in some of the innovative debt structures being employed to finance this growth. I will recap the report's findings and then turn to a discussion of what economic research can tell us about the benefits and risks of integrating AI into financial markets, focusing on wholesale trading. Next, I will examine the potential benefits and risks of AI's effect on cybersecurity and then finally consider what AI might mean for consumer and investor protection.

The AI Investment Boom Anyone watching the news or their retirement plans these past couple of weeks is aware of the questions that investors have raised about the sustainability of the AI investment boom. I should issue the usual disclaimer here that policymakers on the Federal Reserve Board do not target levels of financial markets. Markets go up, and markets go down, and I assiduously avoid commenting on the ups and downs in markets. We do assess longer-term issues that relate to financial stability, and the latest FSR covers several.

In a previous speech, I discussed three different scenarios summarizing the wide range of possible outcomes for how much AI could alter the economy.2 In one possible scenario among several, even if AI turns out to be a transformative innovation that vastly improves productivity, a key question is whether investors will see returns on the AI buildout on a timeline and to an extent consistent with their expectations or whether a different outcome could lead to a significant repricing. The potential investment losses that could result from a large-scale repricing could lower output growth in two ways: first, from the direct effect of a drop in investment, which is a component of gross domestic product; and, second, from the knock-on effects of this loss of wealth in lowering consumer and potentially business spending. As discussed in the latest FSR, the equity premium, a rough measure of the additional return that investors require for holding stocks relative to risk-free bonds, is at low levels relative to historical norms, though not nearly as low as the levels reached during the dot-com stock market boom.3 This is just one indicator to assess where broad measures of equity valuations are relative to historical norms.

items.t: Boris Vujčić: Risks and resilience in the euro area financial system
body: It is my great pleasure to open this year's Frankfurt Euro Finance Week. This event provides a timely opportunity to reflect on the state of the euro area financial system and the challenges ahead. It also comes just two days before the ECB publishes its latest Financial Stability Review (FSR). My key message today is that Europe needs more market-based finance. At the same time, however, a larger role for non-banks must go hand in hand with stronger system-wide safeguards.

While most risks identified in the FSR have been on our radar for quite some time, two stand out very prominently compared to the situation a year ago. These relate to developments in artificial intelligence (AI) and sovereign debt markets.

In our assessment a year ago, AI-related vulnerabilities were fundamentally associated with stretched valuations in global stock markets and the risk that market sentiment could shift abruptly. At present however, while the risk of market repricing, rather than abating, has further increased, AI-related risks to system-wide stability now stem from a range of additional factors – the expansion of external funding from equity to debt markets, concentration of exposures, quickening AI adoption and potential cyberattacks.

In fact, rapid advances in AI models’ cyber capabilities raise risks that have systemic implications. So too does the high concentration of third-party providers of critical services (notably of information and communications technology systems) on which euro area banks and financial intermediaries rely. An early-release FSR special feature published today explores this further.

Concerns about sovereign debt sustainability have been present throughout recent years, reflecting elevated public debt levels and persistently weak fiscal fundamentals in some euro area countries. Sovereign debt fragilities have further increased on both sides of the Atlantic, and are among the factors driving up long-term yields. The risk of global spillovers has also increased. Risks are compounded by inflation concerns, a notable rise in debt issuance by hyperscalers, growing government financing needs, a more price-sensitive investor base, heightened policy and geopolitical uncertainty, and longer-term structural challenges.

Turning to economic activity, over the past year, the euro area economy has proven remarkably resilient in the face of multiple challenges. Economic growth continued to expand in the third quarter of this year, although less dynamically than in the previous quarter.

But the ongoing war in the Middle East continues to push energy prices up, leading to high energy inflation. At the same time, trade policy uncertainty has not abated significantly. Headline inflation in the euro area increased to 4% in October, from 3.8% in September, mainly due to higher energy prices. Underlying inflation has remained broadly stable and wages are not showing a material response at this stage. Overall, recent energy price developments may push inflation higher, while weaker confidence and rising borrowing costs should partially contain this by weighing on growth.

The adverse impact of the energy shock on economic growth has been partly offset by an upbeat AI narrative. But the market correction following the US mid-term elections earlier this month, although contained, serves as a reminder to remain cautious about AI valuations.
Three developments and related sources of risk and vulnerability for euro area financial stability stand out.

First, artificial intelligence. The rapid expansion of AI is creating new challenges for financial stability. Growing debt and equity exposures to AI-linked firms are raising concerns about market concentration, overly optimistic earnings expectations and potential credit risks.

The scale of firms’ financing needs across the AI supply chain is unprecedented. Large cloud and AI infrastructure providers are increasingly turning to debt markets, with issuance volumes reaching record highs this year. Borrowing is likely to increase further, as cumulative capital expenditure by major US technology firms is projected to reach USD 5.5 trillion by 2030.

items.t: Jefferson, New Technology, Old Questions: Productivity Puzzles and the Macroeconomy
items.x: Speech At the University of California, San Diego Economic Roundtable, San Diego, California
body: Thank you, Jim, for that kind introduction, and thank you to UC San Diego for hosting me.1 It is a pleasure to be speaking to this group that includes students, faculty, and business leaders. The topics I want to focus on today are relevant for all of us: How could rapid technological change affect our economy, and what could that mean for monetary policy?

I will start by discussing an earlier period of major technological advances and what lessons we might distill from it for the current juncture. Next, I will turn to what evidence we have regarding the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI).2 I will consider how widely these tools are being used, in which sectors, and what recent research tells us about their potential effects on productivity. Then, I will consider the implications of rapid technological change for the economy more broadly, including for aggregate supply and demand, for inflation, and for the labor market. Finally, I will discuss briefly my thinking about the economic outlook and monetary policy.

Productivity Puzzles: Then and Now Nobel Prize-winning economist Robert Solow famously wrote in 1987 that "you can see the computer age everywhere but in the productivity statistics."3 He may have been expecting too much from the computers he saw. While 32 percent of workers used computers at work in 1989, the computers were not very powerful. To illustrate, the processor in your phone today can do about as many calculations per second as 10 million 1987 vintage personal computers (PCs).4 In the aggregate, national spending on computers—shown in figure 1—was barely detectable at the time, despite PCs being an important part of the zeitgeist.5 Ten years later, computer investment had taken off and some observers, notably Chairman Greenspan, believed they could see it in the productivity statistics, though the link between the two was only established later.6 Investment in information technology (IT) capital—computers, software, and communications equipment—increased the annual growth rate of labor productivity about 3/4 percentage point in the late 1990s.7

While that expansion of the IT capital stock directly boosted worker productivity, there was more than that to the IT boom. Businesses also reorganized their operations around computers, which further supported productivity growth. Advancements in technology changed the cost of creating, storing, and communicating information and provided an opportunity for firms to rethink their scope, scale, and production functions.8 E-commerce, a wave of globalization, and software in the cloud eventually emerged from that process. One sign that reorganization was beneficial and significant was the rapid rise in the amount of output per unit of input outside the IT sector in the early 2000s. That productivity growth was not purely due to investing in more capital; instead, it also reflected increases in what economists call total factor productivity, or TFP.9

The seeds of the 1990s productivity boom were planted long before Solow's observations in 1987. Basic research that laid the foundations for modern computing included the invention of the transistor in 1947 and the Fortran compiler in 1954. For decades, the applied research by firms that followed yielded practical applications for these advances, relentlessly improving information technology.

items.t: Agencies extend comment period for proposed third-party risk management guidance
body: The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, the Federal Reserve Board, the National Credit Union Administration, and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency today announced that they will extend, until December 16, the comment period for proposed guidance on managing risks associated with third-party relationships. Comments on the proposal were originally due November 16.

The proposed guidance reflects the agencies' supervisory experience and lessons learned from examining financial institutions' third-party risk management practices. It is intended to help banks and credit unions tailor their risk management practices to the risks associated with individual third-party relationships. The proposed guidance takes a principles-based approach and, like all supervisory guidance, is non-binding.

When finalized, the federal bank regulatory agencies plan to rescind existing third-party risk management guidance and replace it with the finalized guidance to promote consistency and prudent innovation in the banking industry. NCUA also plans to rescind its existing third-party risk management guidance and will conduct its own reviews to update related guidance as needed.

Also today, the Federal Reserve Board separately announced that it will extend, until December 16, the comment period on a proposed third-party risk management guide specifically for Federal Reserve-supervised traditional community banks.

items.t: Isabel Schnabel: Made in Europe
body: We are living through a period of radical transformation. Technological progress is accelerating alongside profound geopolitical shifts, rewriting the rules that have governed global growth, trade and security for decades.[1]

In this polarised world, Europe is often portrayed as a continent in decline, squeezed between geopolitical rivals, held back by excessive regulation and struggling to keep pace with rapid technological change.
In my remarks this morning, I will argue that although this narrative is appealing in its simplicity, it is misleading.

By many measures, Europe is among the regions with the highest quality of life, grounded in strong institutions, a high degree of social protection and an exceptional capacity to adapt in times of crisis.
Europe can build on these fundamentals to become even stronger.

I will explain that the key is to unlock the full potential of the Single Market – one of Europe’s most powerful assets – to deliver what Europe lacks today: not talent, not ideas, not research – but scale.
A 28th regime would be a true game changer in this respect.

By giving firms seamless access to the entire European market, it would provide the scale needed to convert innovation into economic growth. It would allow Europe to compete as one economy rather than 27, and help create something Europe has long been missing: a true “Made in Europe” brand.
Europe stands out globally for its quality of life, built on strong economic, social and institutional foundations.

Happiness and life satisfaction in Europe consistently rank among the highest in the world (Slide 2). This goes beyond income or wealth – it reflects the broader conditions that allow people to live secure, fulfilling and prosperous lives.
Social protection, accessible public infrastructure, high-quality public education and family support help turn economic prosperity into tangible improvements in people’s lives.[2]
Health outcomes are particularly revealing here.

A child born in Spain or Italy can expect to live five years longer than a child born in the United States (Slide 3), despite the United States spending a far larger share of GDP on healthcare than any other advanced economy. Even among the wealthiest Americans, mortality rates are merely at the level of the poorest populations in parts of Europe.[3]

Europeans also benefit from strong institutions. A growing share of the world’s population now lives under de facto autocratic rule, while attacks on democratic freedoms continue at an alarming pace (Slide 4).

Against this backdrop, Europe’s continued commitment to democracy, the rule of law and institutional checks and balances underpin trust and policy credibility, while independent media ensure accountability and transparency.
These institutions and principles give people confidence in their future and in the fairness of society, even in the face of adversity.

So, throughout its history, Europe has made deliberate choices about the kind of society it wants to be. But while these choices have resulted in better life outcomes, they have also weighed on GDP per capita, adjusted for the cost of living, which is one of the most used indicators of economic prosperity.
By this measure, the euro area ranks below other advanced economies (Slide 5).[4]

Part of this difference reflects the fact that some euro area economies are still catching up, mainly in eastern Europe. These countries are mostly growing rapidly, but their incomes remain below the euro area average, which dampens the headline number.
Yet, a substantial gap remains even for the more advanced euro area economies. Interpreting this gap requires careful analysis along three dimensions.[5]
First, a large part of the gap in income levels reflects less work rather than less productive work.
On average, an employee in the United States works around 40 days more per year than an employee in the euro area (Slide 6, left-hand side).[6]

items.t: Federal Reserve Board announces pricing, effective January 1, 2027, for payment services the Federal Reserve Banks provide to banks and credit unions, and changes to streamline and adjust their check…
body: The Federal Reserve Board on Thursday announced pricing, effective January 1, 2027, for payment services the Federal Reserve Banks provide to banks and credit unions, such as the clearing of checks, automated clearing house (ACH) transactions, instant payments, and wholesale payment and settlement services.

By law, the Federal Reserve must establish fees to recover the costs, including imputed costs, of providing payment services over the long run. The Federal Reserve expects to recover 101.5 percent of actual and imputed expenses in 2027, including the return on equity that would have been earned if a private-sector firm provided the services. Overall, price changes for 2027 will result in an estimated 1.4 percent average price increase for established, mature services.

In addition, the Federal Reserve Banks announced changes to streamline and adjust their check services. As described in the request for information on check services issued last year, the volume of checks processed by the Federal Reserve Banks is declining, but checks remain an important payment instrument for many consumers and businesses. The changes were informed by public feedback and ensure that the Federal Reserve Banks continue to provide check services efficiently. The adjustments include optimizing check processing windows during low-volume periods, increasing fees that banks and credit unions pay to process checks, and other operational updates. These changes do not impact consumers' and businesses' ability to pay with or receive checks and only impact how banks and credit unions process checks with Federal Reserve Banks.

The entire 2027 fee schedule for all of the Federal Reserve's payment services is published on FRBservices.org®. Additional information on the Federal Reserve's payments services, including service usage statistics, is available on the Board's website.
